Motivation

Dr. Simon Müller

2026-11-22

Source: vignettes/distance_measures.rmd
distance_measures.rmd

Objective

Define a Distance Measure for Numerical and Categorical Features

Let xi=(xi1,⋯,xip)Tx_i = \left(x_i^1,\cdots,x_i^p\right)^T and xj=(xj1,⋯,xjp)Tx_j = \left(x_j^1,\cdots,x_j^p\right)^T be the feature vectors of two distinct patients ii and jj. A first rough idea may be to calculate the L1−L_1-norm of this two feature vectors: ∥xi−xj∥L1=1p∑k=1p|xik−xjk| \|x_i - x_j\|_{L_1}=\frac{1}{p}\sum\limits_{k=1}^p|x_i^k - x_j^k|

However, this naive approach arises from some problems:

  1. This measure is well-defined for numerical features but not for categorical features, such as gender (male/female). We need a method to define the distance for categorical variables.

  2. |xik−xjk||x_i^k - x_j^k| is not scale-invariant, meaning that if one changes the unit of measurement (e.g., from meters to centimeters), the contribution of this feature would increase by a factor of 100. Features with large values will dominate the distance.

  3. All features are treated equally, which may not reflect their actual importance. For example, in the case of lung cancer, the patient’s smoking status (no/yes) seems more relevant than the city they live in.

This package addresses these issues by deriving a weighted distance from regression model coefficients, which naturally handles mixed feature types and reflects each feature’s importance.

Weighted Distance Measure

To address the challenges discussed earlier, we need to perform two steps:

  1. Generalize the L1-distance to handle different variable types, including numerical and categorical features.

  2. Assign appropriate weights to each feature to:

    a. eliminate the dependency on the scale of the variables,

    1. account for varying importance across features, and
    2. consider the impact size of each feature.

By incorporating these modifications, we arrive at the following weighted distance measure:

d(xi,xj)=∑k=1p|α(xik,xjk)d(xik,xjk)| d(x_i, x_j) = \sum\limits_{k=1}^p |\alpha(x_i^k, x_j^k) d(x_i^k, x_j^k)|

The weighted distance measure now includes weights α(xik,xjk)\alpha(x_i^k, x_j^k), which are determined based on the training data. In the next section, we will discuss how to obtain these weights and effectively compute the weighted distance measure for mixed data types and varying feature importance.

Statistical Model

Let α(xik,xjk)\alpha(x_i^k, x_j^k) the weights and d(xik,xjk)d(x_i^k, x_j^k) the distance for feature kk and observation ii and jj. We will define them as:

If feature kk is numerical, then

d(xik,xjk)=xik−xjkd(x_i^k, x_j^k) = x_i^k - x_j^k and

α(xik,xjk)=β̂k\alpha(x_i^k, x_j^k) = \hat{\beta}_k

If feature kk is categorical, then

d(xik,xjk)=1 when xik≠xjk else 0d(x_i^k, x_j^k) = 1 \text{ when } x_i^k \neq x_j^k \text{ else } 0 and α(xik,xjk)=β̂k(xik)−β̂k(xjk),\alpha(x_i^k, x_j^k) = \hat{\beta}_k^{(x_i^k)} - \hat{\beta}_k^{(x_j^k)},

where β̂k(l)\hat{\beta}_k^{(l)} is the coefficient of level ll (zero for the reference level) in a regression model (linear, logistic, or CPH model). The regression coefficients thus serve as weights that reflect each feature’s importance and scale.

Contribution Space

Both cases are special cases of one definition. Let ct(x)=Xt(x)β̂tc_t(x) = X_t(x)\hat{\beta}_t be the contribution of model term tt to the linear predictor, where Xt(x)X_t(x) are the columns of the design matrix that belong to term tt and β̂t\hat{\beta}_t their coefficients. The package computes

d(xi,xj)=∑t|ct(xi)−ct(xj)|. d(x_i, x_j) = \sum\limits_{t} |c_t(x_i) - c_t(x_j)|.

For a numerical main effect, ct(x)=β̂kxkc_t(x) = \hat{\beta}_k x^k; for a categorical one, ct(x)=β̂k(xk)c_t(x) = \hat{\beta}_k^{(x^k)}, so the distance is exactly the weighted distance above. The definition also covers any other term of an rms model: splines such as rcs(age, 4), polynomials and interactions. Two cases are then close if the model assigns them similar contributions, even if a non-linear effect makes equal differences in a variable count differently in different ranges.

explain_match() reports the terms |ct(xi)−ct(xj)||c_t(x_i) - c_t(x_j)| and their share of the distance, which shows why two cases match.

Random Forests

Proximity Measure

Two observations ii and jj are considered more similar when the fraction of trees in which they share the same terminal node is close to one (Breiman, 2002). With proximity

p(xi,xj)=1T∑t=1T1[xi and xj share the same terminal node in tree t], p(x_i, x_j) = \frac{1}{T}\sum\limits_{t=1}^T 1_{[x_i \text{ and } x_j \text{ share the same terminal node in tree } t]},

where TT is the number of trees, the distance is

d(xi,xj)=1−p(xi,xj). d(x_i, x_j) = \sqrt{1 - p(x_i, x_j)}.

A drawback of this measure is that the decision is binary, meaning that potentially similar observations might be counted as dissimilar. For example, suppose a final cut-off is consistently made around age 58, and observation 1 has an age of 56 while observation 2 has an age of 60. In this case, the distance between observation 1 and observation 2 would be the same as the distance between observation 1 and an observation with an age of 80. This limitation makes the proximity measure less sensitive to small differences between observations, potentially affecting the overall analysis of similarity.

Out-of-Bag and RF-GAP Proximities

The original proximity is biased for training cases: a tree is grown until its leaves are small, so cases in a tree’s bootstrap sample tend to share leaves with each other. Two variants avoid this (proximity_type in proximity_distance(), distance_random_forest() and RFModel$set_distance_method()):

  • OOB: only the trees in which both observations are out-of-bag are counted, and TT is replaced by the number of these trees.

  • RF-GAP (Rhodes, Cutler & Moon, 2023): for a query qq and a training case jj, p(q,j)=1|Sq|∑t∈Sqcj(t)1[j∈vq(t)]|Mq(t)|, p(q, j) = \frac{1}{|S_q|}\sum\limits_{t \in S_q} \frac{c_j(t)\, 1_{[j \in v_q(t)]}}{|M_q(t)|}, where SqS_q are the trees in which qq is out-of-bag (all trees for new data), vq(t)v_q(t) is the terminal node of qq in tree tt, cj(t)c_j(t) is the in-bag count of jj in tree tt, and |Mq(t)||M_q(t)| is the total in-bag count in vq(t)v_q(t).

The RF-GAP proximities of a query sum to one over the training cases, and the proximity-weighted average of the training outcomes equals the forest’s (out-of-bag) prediction. Retrieval with RF-GAP therefore uses the same notion of similarity as the forest’s predictions. Because the proximities are small, RF-GAP distances lie close to 1; only their order matters. Both variants need the in-bag counts, which RFModel keeps by default (keep.inbag = TRUE).

Depth Measure: A modified proximity measure

In contrast to the proximity measure, the depth measure takes into account the number of edges between the terminal nodes of two observations, not only whether they coincide. It is summed over all trees:

d(xi,xj)=∑t=1Tgij(t), d(x_i, x_j) = \sum\limits_{t=1}^T g_{ij}(t),

where gij(t)g_{ij}(t) is the number of edges on the path between the terminal nodes of observation ii and jj in tree tt, i.e. the sum of their distances to the deepest common ancestor. Observations that end up in neighbouring leaves are close, observations in distant parts of the tree are far apart. This is the default distance of RFModel.

The edge counts are computed on demand from each tree’s structure, so the cost grows with the number of pairs and the tree depth, not with the number of nodes.

For more details and a thorough explanation of the depth measure, refer to the publication by Englund and Verikas: “A novel approach to estimate proximity in a random forest: An exploratory study.”

References

  • Breiman, L. (2002). Manual on setting up, using, and understanding random forests V3.1.
  • Dippon, J. et al. (2002). A statistical approach to case based reasoning, with application to breast cancer data.
  • Englund, C. and Verikas, A. (2012). A novel approach to estimate proximity in a random forest: An exploratory study.
  • Rhodes, J. S., Cutler, A. and Moon, K. R. (2023). Geometry- and Accuracy-Preserving Random Forest Proximities.
